children: BlackRock remains structurally overweight on India and expects foreign investor flows to return once uncertainty around the US midterm elections and West Asia tensions subsides, according to Ben Powell, Chief APAC & Middle East Investment Strategist at the BlackRock Investment Institute.

Powell said India's long-term investment case remains intact despite short-term global risks weighing on investor sentiment. India is in a unique position as household savings increasingly move into financial assets such as equities and bonds.
This, he says, creates a domestic pool of capital that can support economic expansion at a time when governments and companies across the world are competing for funding.
BlackRock has also published research highlighting India's economic growth and its ability to finance that growth through rising household participation in financial markets.

Globally, Powell said, markets are closely watching whether the US midterm elections could influence artificial intelligence (AI)-related regulation, particularly around data centre expansion. While elections remain difficult to predict, he said investors are focused on what policy outcomes could mean for AI infrastructure investment.

[faq type="interview" title="This is an edited transcript of the interview."][ques][/ques][ans][/ans][/faq][faq type="interview"][ques]The big story is crude posting a 6% gain last week, the third consecutive weekly gain. This morning, it's eased off a bit to $115 per barrel, but it's still very high. It was also a tense weekend in terms of the news flow. President Trump also heightened the rhetoric by saying, "Do I make a deal with them or do I finish them off?" So please summarise your thoughts. What's happening in West Asia, and how do things stand right now?[/ques][ans]It feels like the world is holding its breath as we head up to a couple of interesting elections, in Israel and some others. But obviously, the big one is in roughly 10 days' time, the US midterms. So, we're in this very awkward moment whereby it's a little bit of a ‘wait and see’. The rhetoric is escalating naturally. Markets are appropriately nervous that that rhetoric can escalate into something more real. So, it's quite natural that risk is pausing or even selling off a little bit. That's why we at BlackRock downgraded our US equity call a couple of weeks back to reflect these tensions, which are clearly persisting and driving markets. And as I say, it's hard to see beyond the midterms. So, we've got at least 10 days of complexity and uncertainty. That's just kind of where we're stuck right now.[/ans][/faq][faq type="interview"][ques]I'll get to the oil bid in just a bit, but since you brought up the midterms, what's the sharp takeaway that will matter for markets after the third?[/ques][ans]It's a very interesting election. What seems to be happening more recently, in terms of polling and so forth, is that the Democrats seem to be doing better and better. So of course, we'll have to wait and see. But there is some chance that the Democratic Party ends up with both the House of Representatives and the Senate, and that could lead to a quite complicated situation of divided government. Now, divided government isn't particularly new; that happens from time to time. But it would potentially be a moment of divided government when, frankly, tensions and sentiment on all sides in the American political system are very high. That has some interesting consequences politically, but for us in markets, I guess the big one is: what does it mean for the AI trade? Could there be more regulatory uncertainty vis-à-vis data center build-out and so forth? So, clearly elections are important. Elections in the biggest economy and, frankly, the most important country in the world are definitely very important. The specific issue for us in markets is much more practical. What does it mean for AI data center build-out, and in turn, what does that mean for markets? And, again, there's a few things going on. We've just talked about the heightened tensions here in the West Asia and so on. So that's definitely relevant. But I really think markets are kind of holding their breath in multiple dimensions, including whether there is some risk against the data center build-out, and could that risk be changed in any way by the fallout from the forthcoming US midterm elections?[/ans][/faq][faq type="interview"][ques]Two questions. One is the consensus or the base case for you that the Democrats win?[/ques][ans]It's very close to call. So, for now, it very much looks like the House of Representatives, as you know, has two kinds of political arenas in play. So, the House looks like it's very plausibly switching to the Democrats. The Senate's also very close, and as you know, in these elections we're talking about a few thousand, maybe a few hundred, votes going one way or the other. So, we, from an investment perspective, don't want to hang our hats on this. We're focused on earnings and fundamentals. But I always answer if I'm asked a straight question. So, I think we should be at least aware of this chance, and the market clearly is more aware of the chance of the Democrats taking both the House and the Senate in a week and a bit's time.[/ans][/faq][faq type="interview"][ques]If that happens, you mentioned the data center risk and data center build-out. Are Democrats opposed to the pace of the data center build-out? Is that a political position they've taken?[/ques][ans]I think there's a genuine political debate to be had in all countries. And what's interesting in the US is that this happens largely at the state level. So, we've already seen - I think it's 25 or even more states. That number definitely needs fact-checking, but it's a meaningful number of states. They have already imposed something like a data center moratorium, so this is already happening, and we're seeing this complexity play out. And it seems to be something that many voters are concerned about. So, it's very natural that political parties of all stripes are thinking about this, as they should be, reflecting the demands and needs of their people. So, I do think the big AI companies have got a job to do in trying to reassure citizens that a data center coming to a neighbourhood near them is not a bad thing and might even be a good thing. But clearly, that has not succeeded so far. Many American citizens are very cautious about this, and I do think that is an aspect of what's going to play out in the coming election period.[/ans][/faq][faq type="interview"][ques]But before we wind up this conversation, a lot of our viewers will want to understand your stance on India. I think you've taken note of the kind of flows we have seen from domestic investors. The FIIs remain sellers, but maybe not as much as what we saw a month or so ago. Give and take everything—the high-frequency data on the ground, and the time-wise, price-wise correction we have seen in the Indian markets—would you be a little bit more optimistic about the prospects?[/ques][ans]We're still structurally overweight on India on a strategic horizon, and we've written a paper that we're publishing today, where we're talking about not just the growth, which is very well understood. India's astonishing growth, even in the face of the challenges over the last six or nine months, is very noteworthy. The IMF has upgraded growth and so on. So, the growth story is ongoing and very strong. What we're focusing on today is how that growth story is going to be financed. So, we're seeing huge competition for capital all over the world. Western governments have got very large deficits. That's maybe not new. What is new is the AI hyperscaler build-out needing billions, maybe even trillions, of dollars. So, who has got money is a very important strategic question. India's got money, and what we're expecting to see over the next few years is more and more household savings. Again, normal people channelling more of their savings into financial assets, such as stocks and bonds, which hopefully will be good for them. They should reap market returns over time. But it's also good for the Indian economy because we're seeing this world, which is struggling, or at least questioning where we can find capital. If it is the case, and we think this is the case at BlackRock, that India can mobilise more of its household savings, that should lead to a win-win. Again, a win for those investors, and also a win for the Indian economy because that's a fantastic source of funding, which is not available in other countries around the world.[/ans][/faq][faq type="interview"][ques]What about foreign funding? Do you see foreign flows coming back to India?[/ques][ans]I do. As I mentioned, there's an awful lot going on in the short term. So, I think it's quite natural that everyone is kind of chickening out a little bit in the short term, not just of India, but as a general risk-off call: West Asia question mark, US midterm question mark. There's always a lot of question marks, but it feels like there are many at the moment, and they're big. So, the foreigners will continue to wait and see until we get through the US midterms. Once we're through that, and hopefully with a little bit more certainty on the West Asia side, as we look around the world for growth opportunities, great companies, and so forth, India is clearly on the list. So, we're not quite there yet, I don't think, unfortunately. Again, that's not an India comment specifically. That's more of a risk comment. But I really think if we can get through the midterms, the sun will come up. There will be good companies delivering earnings at attractive valuations, and risk appetite will return, but perhaps maybe not until next week, as a broad statement.[/ans][/faq]

title: BlackRock stays overweight on India, sees domestic savings powering long-term market growth
